title: Variables

cells.text: A **variable** is a name that stores a value, like a labelled box. `price = 60` means "store 60 under the name price". In Python, `=` means **store**, not "equals" like in maths. The name goes on the left and the value on the right.

cells.prompt: Press Run to store 60 in price, then print it.

cells.text: Notice there are no quotes in `print(price)`. Without quotes, Python looks up what's stored in price. Cells also **remember** variables, so price still works in every cell below this one.

cells.prompt: This cell uses price from the cell above. Press Run.
Careful with the quotes this time. What will this print? Pick one, then press Run.

cells.text: With quotes, `"price"` is just the word price, so Python prints it as text. You can also **change** a variable. Python reads code top to bottom, so `x = x + 2` means "take x, add 2, and store the result back in x".

cells.prompt: Follow the code line by line. What will this print? Pick one, then press Run.

cells.text: Variables can store text too. Just put the text in quotes, like `name = "Raph"`.

cells.prompt: Replace ___ with the name of any game, in quotes, then press Run.
hints: The game name needs quotes around it, because it's text.

cells.prompt: Your turn. price is still 60 from earlier. On the first line, finish copies = so that copies stores 4. On the second line, print price times copies (use * for times). You should see 240.
hints: First line: copies = 4. Second line: put price * copies inside print().

recap: = stores a value under a name. Without quotes, Python uses what's stored; with quotes, it's just text. Cells remember variables, so later cells can use them.
